excerpt: Riley Windeler holds a copy of his recently published children's book Tommy’s Race at Riverside Park in Kamloops. It has been ten years in the making for Riley Windeler who has finally released his first children’s book that he hopes empowers kids in the Cariboo and beyond. The debut author who was born and raised in Horsefly but currently resides in Kamloops has a form of short-limbed dwarfism called Hypochondroplasia. Despite his small stature of four feet and six inches Windeler hasn’t let that stand in the way, serving as inspiration for *Tommy’s Race.* He received a copy of his long awaited work that is illustrated by Nora Kelly of Montreal, Que. from Caitlin Press late last month. “It has been a whole process,” Windeler said of his long awaited book. “Now it’s here and now it’s done.” *Tommy’s Race* is based off of a race from Windeler’s childhood in the small rural community east of Williams Lake. He clearly remembers the end of his first school sports day when he was about six-years-old and his friends crossed the finish line completing the race while he was still half down the field. “That was the first real time it hit me that Ok there’s this difference here,” Windeler said. *Tommy’s Race* begins with a young character named Tommy participating in a similar such race and despite coming in last place later going to a World Dwarf Athletic event after months of training to compete on a level playing field, making friends and having the courage to win. “It’s showing that yes there are these challenges but there’s also opportunities out there between the two,” Windeler said, smiling. Windeler himself persevered while he was younger playing hockey and baseball. While he said he knows he might not have been the best player he remained passionate about the sport and enjoyed playing, being awarded the most inspirational and most dedicated player by the Williams Lake Minor Hockey Association. In an Oct. 22 release on TRU’s website, WLFN Chief Willie Sellars said, “We take great pride in building relationships and partnerships with institutions like Thompson Rivers University, operating within T’exelcemc territory and lifting up both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people across our region.” Sellars further added these partnerships create meaningful opportunities to advance reconciliation, and education is a key part of that work. He said, “By supporting learning, sharing knowledge and creating opportunities for people to better understand one another, we can help build a stronger future for everyone in our region.” The new agreement includes a joint implementation plan to put the new formalized agreement into practice. A Rotary Peace Pole was recently installed in front of Williams Lake City Hall with a gathering and dedication ceremony held Wednesday, Oct. 21. title: GM just did 34,000 years of battery testing in less than a month. Here’s how
description:
Developing new EV battery technology takes years of research. General Motors, for example, says it’s put a decade of effort into lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, batteries, which aren’t yet in any of their vehicles on the road.

But recently, the automaker says it made a big leap in that work. Using computer modeling, GM was able to virtually test more than 300,000 LMR battery pack configurations, advancing from first concept to formal approval in under a month. 

That represents more than 300 million CPU hours, which would take a typical computer 34,000 years, while running 24 hours a day, to complete, according to GM.

GM is leaning into artificial intelligence and virtual simulations to develop its vehicles. That not only speeds up the time to do testing, per the company, but allows it to test more options, rather than picking the best of just a few configurations. 

Those 300,000 formulations, for example, looked at different chemical combinations, temperature cycling, and other approaches to creating a battery cell, Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, told Fast Company. 

“If we had not had the luxury of some of these tools, we would have had to sample more sparsely from what was possible,” he says. 

Speeding up vehicle development

GM is bringing this AI approach beyond battery testing and into all areas of its vehicle development, with the aim of slashing the time it takes to develop a car in half. 

Typically, cars are developed within a four- or five-year time frame. That allows a “limited number” of all kinds of tests, Anderson says, from wind tunnel to crash tests. 

“Now in the virtual world, instead of the X crash test that we could have done, or Y prototypes that could go through, we can run X times 100 and Y times 1000,” he says. 

GM is also working to advance its autonomous driving capabilities with real-world and virtual testing. Hundreds of data-collection vehicles are currently driving across the country collecting 1 million miles of data a month, while virtually, GM systems drive more than 3 billion simulated miles a day.

By cutting vehicle development down to about two years, GM also says it can adapt more quickly to external challenges. Many car makers were counting on Biden-era EV tax credits to help their sales, for example, but then the Trump administration cut those credits. 

Tariffs, the war in Iran’s effect on gas prices, changing regulations, and uneasy consumer sentiments have all added uncertainty to automakers’ future product lineups, which may have been in development for years. 

A shorter development cycle “makes you more agile,” Anderson says. 

LMR batteries in the works

GM wants to be the first automaker to deploy LMR batteries, and Anderson says they’re on track to make that happen. 

LMR batteries can have 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and use a higher amount of less-expensive minerals (like manganese) rather than more of the most expensive minerals like cobalt and nickel. That allows them to offer more range—potentially more than 400 miles—at a lower cost and lighter weight. 

GM is also preparing to roll out its fourth-generation EV platform, which includes not only LMR batteries but a centralized, upgraded computing system, and new electrical work. 

It will have 30% less wiring than GM’s current EVs and 40% fewer parts in its motors and power electronics, which make it lighter and more efficient. 

GM and LG Energy Solution are working on these batteries as part of a joint venture called Ultium Cells. They plan to start commercial production of the LMR battery cells in the U.S. by 2028, at the Ultium Cells facility in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

title: Principles and Practice of Deep Representation Learning
description:
Sam Buchanan, Druv Pai, Peng Wang, Yi Ma, GitHub, Oct 22, 2026

This is "a modern fully open-source textbook exploring why and how deep neural networks learn compact and information-dense representations of high-dimensional real-world data." It's a daunting read - and to be honest, I gave the first chapter a careful read but have only skimmed the rest (though it's now on my virtual bookshelf for future reference). I think people who are serious about understanding how we learn and how machines emulate this should at the very least read that first chapter. It contains what is to my understanding an accurate history of artificial intelligence (including the important early work in computation, cybernetics, and information theory). The aim of the book is to give us a framework that explains how neural networks work to generate intelligence. They authors write, "intelligence is not about collecting all informative data in advance and training a model to memorize their (low-dimensional) distribution. Instead, it requires computational mechanisms that can continuously improve current knowledge of the distribution and acquire new information when needed. A fundamental characteristic of any intelligent being or system - whether an animal, a human, a civilization, or the entire scientific community - is the ability to continuously improve or gain new information or knowledge on its own."

title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
description:
Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation

News today from Anthropic:

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

I'm pleased to note I called this one last December, when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard":

I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF, recently the new home of the MCP specification.

Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to "Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body".

title: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?
description:
With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future

Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit. But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction, something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.

Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company, and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.

title: COP31 to Take Place in Antalya, Turkiye, as SP Architects Adapts Former Expo Grounds
description: The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, under a joint governance model where Türkiye hosts the summit and presidency, while Australia leads the formal negotiations. The conference will bring together national delegations, government representatives, scientists, businesses, and civil society to discuss international climate action, including emissions reduction, adaptation to climate impacts, and climate finance. As countries continue to face the challenges of extreme weather, resource consumption, and the transition to lower-carbon economies, this year's programme includes dedicated discussions on zero waste, energy and transport, and resilient cities. In preparation for the event, SP Architects is adapting the former EXPO 2016 grounds in Antalya to accommodate the conference, with plans for the site to remain in use after it concludes.

title: AI agents spread as job, safety and investment risks draw scrutiny
description:
Companies and governments are adopting AI agents that can carry out tasks, while researchers and policymakers examine their effects on jobs, security and investment. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said he uses agents to summarize internal discussions and track computing use, but humans still make consequential decisions about allocating resources. Google has also introduced agentic AI for public agencies, and the United Arab Emirates plans to shift half of federal government operations and services to autonomous agents within two years.

Stanford University researchers report that employment in AI-exposed software development and customer-service jobs fell by more than 4% this year, while Harvard researchers say current labor-market signals offer little certainty about AI’s longer-term effects. Central bankers are assessing potential effects on wages and productivity, and a University of Hawaiʻi analysis estimates that AI investment and related stock gains have supported U.S. growth and consumer spending.

Security teams report difficulty verifying agents’ answers, and AI infrastructure borrowers, including CoreWeave, face rising credit risks. Center for Internet Security senior director of threat intelligence TJ Sayers said autonomous AI attacks are no longer hypothetical. Agent use remained in single digits across almost every business function, according to the Stanford 2026 AI Index cited by The National.

title: Cleveland-Cliffs announces Hamilton layoffs as Canada, Ontario unveil aid
description:
U.S.-owned steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs announced layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant as Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a C$8.7 billion support package for steel, auto and critical-mineral businesses. The plan also includes up to C$1 billion in federal funding, matched by Ontario, for roads serving the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in northern Ontario.

The U.S. Embassy in Canada separately accused Canadian politicians of trying to influence the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, citing remarks about retaliatory tariffs and political meetings. Carney and Ford rejected the allegation. The embassy also cited 11 Canadians charged with voting illegally but did not link them to the Canadian government. A parliamentary petition calling for U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra’s removal had gathered more than 275,000 signatures.

Down at Byron Louie Memorial Park for Williams Lake First Nation's pumpkin patch on Friday, Oct. 16 were Crystal Wells with her daughter Harper. The fifth annual pumpkin patch by Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) was the biggest one yet drawing hundreds of families to celebrate the fall season with games, hotdogs and a pumpkin to take home. This was the first year the event supporting social development programming was held at Byron Louie Memorial Park located south of Williams Lake in Sugar Cane. In 2025 the pumpkin patch was held outside the Thompson Rivers University campus in Williams Lake. WLFN manager of marketing and communications Brandon Hoffman said chief and council wanted to have it closer to community while within walking distance and still attracting as many visitors as possible. The three hour event also included family photos, bouncy castle and vendors selling lemonade, bannock, ribbon skirts and more. Organizations such as Knucwentwecw Society and Denisiqi Services Society provided activities and games including spooky decorated oreos and a ring toss. Several wooden photo stand-ins were specifically made for the day by WLFN member Michaela Gilbert. Hoffman confirmed this year’s pumpkin patch was the largest one drawing over 800 people, including more than 125 WLFN members. The remaining few pumpkins at the end of the night from Sugar Cane Ranch and Save-On-Foods didn’t go to waste with WLFN ensuring they all found useful homes.

title: Uganda targets 10,000 tractors in five-year mechanization push
description:
Uganda plans to deploy 10,000 tractors over five years to expand mechanized farming, Agriculture Minister Frank Tumwebaze told Parliament on Oct. 21. The strategy proposes 21 mechanization centers and a cost-sharing model involving the government, commercial farmers and producer groups. Tumwebaze said dependence on manual labor and unpredictable weather constrain productivity, while machinery could help farmers cultivate more land and support value-added production.

Kubota and autonomy-software company Agtonomy are extending a pilot to automate orchard work such as spraying, mowing and underplant cultivation. In the United States, drone-treated acreage grew to 16.4 million acres in 2025. Equipment makers have also introduced higher-capacity grain conveyors designed to reduce harvest handling time.

title: Musk endorsement raises scrutiny risk for Tesla-SpaceX merger talks
description:
Elon Musk’s public support for combining Tesla, the electric-vehicle maker he leads, with SpaceX, the rocket and AI company he also leads, has raised concerns among people involved in the talks that shareholder scrutiny could delay negotiations by several weeks. Independent board committees are still reviewing the proposed deal, and no terms have been agreed.

The companies are considering several structures, including a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla, a new holding company or an all-stock transaction, according to people familiar with the discussions. SpaceX approached Tesla in recent weeks, and both companies have hired advisers. People involved in the talks are concerned that Musk’s endorsement could raise questions about whether the deal would protect Tesla shareholders’ interests.

Tesla’s third-quarter net income fell 43% to $787 million while revenue was roughly flat at $28 billion. Tesla reported $1.5 billion in free cash flow and cut its 2026 capital-spending forecast to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion. Any merger would still need approval from holders of at least half of all Tesla shares.

title: Apple Ordered to Open iPhone to Rival App Stores in Australia
description:
Australia's Federal Court today ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads, and alternative payment services for Australian users from March 1, 2027.


The orders follow the court's August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by restricting app distribution and payment options. They cover users whose Apple Account region is Australia, with Apple Developer Program members worldwide able to participate.

Apple must let users find, download, install, and update apps through competing marketplaces and websites without charging for access or obstructing their use. Developers must receive the necessary tools on substantially the same terms as for App Store distribution, and Apple cannot penalize them for using competing stores or payment services.

Developers will also be able to offer alternative payments and link to other ways to pay, including within ‌App Store‌ apps. Apple cannot require them to offer its own purchasing system alongside alternatives, report those transactions, or allow Apple to audit them. Developers can offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple preventing them.

The ruling also limits Apple's ability to collect fees on those purchases. It cannot charge for purchases through alternative payment services or websites in apps distributed outside the ‌App Store‌. For ‌App Store‌ apps, fees are capped at the equivalent charge for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine, reasonable additional costs Apple incurs for digital purchases.

Apple also cannot make alternative distribution conditional on developers offering content purchased elsewhere through its own payment system.

Security checks will remain. Apps downloaded outside the ‌App Store‌ must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and be notarized by Apple or a qualified third party. However, Apple cannot impose disproportionate installation barriers or otherwise obstruct alternative distribution. Additional security requirements for competing payments must be necessary and proportionate, with developers given an explanation in advance.

Apple can remove or disable externally installed apps only in specified cases involving harmful content, genuine security risks, or legal requirements. It cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones, but does not have to distribute competing stores through the ‌App Store‌.

Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and ‌App Store‌ security.

The changes take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for a court-approved extension until May 3.

title: Canada commits billions to steel upgrades as Hamilton layoffs loom
description:
U.S.-owned steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs confirmed layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant on Oct. 21 as Canada announced a C$8.7 billion ($6.2 billion) package for the steel, auto and critical-mineral industries. Hundreds of workers at Hamilton-based Stelco face imminent cuts; Cleveland-Cliffs has cited market pressures, including U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel.

The five-year plan allocates C$5.2 billion to steelmakers and C$2.5 billion to automakers. Steel funding is intended to help mills upgrade equipment and supply Canadian and other non-U.S. markets, while auto aid is meant to accelerate the shift to electric-vehicle production. Ottawa is also putting C$1 billion toward roads to northern Ontario’s Ring of Fire mineral region, matching a previous provincial commitment.

title: US orders non-emergency embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia after attacks
description:
The U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, Oct. 21, after deadly attacks on airports and energy infrastructure disrupted travel. The order covers only U.S. missions in Saudi Arabia, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said, disputing reports that the department had ordered wider departures. Four U.S. officials told Reuters that family members at other Gulf missions would also be asked to leave.

Saudi authorities initially said an attack at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight; later updates raised the death toll to two. Separately, debris from an intercepted drone targeting Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil field killed two foreign workers and injured two others. The Energy Ministry said the incident did not affect oil-field operations.

The drawdown follows a sharp rise in attacks by Yemen’s Houthi movement and a U.S. security alert warning of possible further strikes and travel disruption. U.S. government personnel in Saudi Arabia now need special authorization to use any airport, while authorities assess damage at Dammam.

title: South Korea central bank holds rate at 3%, signals November hike
description:
The Bank of Korea (BOK) kept its benchmark rate at 3% on Thursday, Oct. 22, after raising it by a quarter-point in both July and August. The unanimous decision gives policymakers time to assess those increases and economic risks. The bank said the timing of future hikes would depend on inflation, growth and financial stability.

The central bank said growth this year and next is likely to exceed its August forecasts of 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively, while September inflation remained at 2.9%, above its 2% target. Strong semiconductor exports and rising oil prices are among the factors shaping its outlook. Analysts expect another quarter-point increase at the next policy meeting on Nov. 26; the bank will first review third-quarter growth and October inflation data.

title: A timeout doesn’t mean an operation failed. It means you don’t know the outcome.
description:
A trap I see people fall into when implementing resiliency is assuming a timeout means something failed.

Let’s imagine you’re buying some very expensive concert tickets online. Obviously, you’re trying to catch the latest Taylor Swift tour.

You’ve picked your seats, entered your information, and clicked checkout. Then the page times out…

Do you immediately go back and buy the tickets again? Probably not.

First, you check whether your card was charged. You look for a confirmation email. Maybe you check your account to see if the tickets are there.

Only after confirming nothing happened do you decide whether to try again.

Now imagine the same scenario, but you’re just looking at tour dates. When the page times out, do you refresh? Absolutely.

So why is one safe to unthinkingly retry and the other isn’t? Because one scenario has an operation that could be painful if performed twice.

A timeout on a checkout page doesn’t mean the operation failed; it just means you don’t know the outcome. And when you don’t know the outcome, a blind retry is a terrible idea.

The Blind Retry Resiliency Trap

Blind retries are a trap I see teams fall into when trying to make their systems more resilient. They treat all requests the same.

Maybe they do so by adopting a retry library or configuring automatic retries in their service mesh. Or maybe they ask an AI coding agent to add retry logic to every outbound request.

But some requests need more than a retry.

If you’re querying for data and the request times out, retrying might be perfectly fine. But what if you're posting a financial transaction? Just because your client timed out doesn’t mean the transaction failed.

Before implementing retries, ask yourself what happens if the first attempt actually succeeded.

Sometimes You Need to Know What Happened

For requests that perform operations with side effects, you need a way to manage that uncertainty. Maybe you query the downstream system to determine whether the transaction completed before retrying.

Or maybe the operation is idempotent. If every attempt includes a transaction ID and the downstream system recognizes duplicates before performing the operation again, great—retry.

The key is, the right approach depends on the use case and the implementation at hand.

Doing Nothing Can Be Just As Bad

It might be tempting to read my warnings above and think, “ok I just won’t retry operations that make changes.”

But that can also cause problems.

Imagine a point-of-sale system initiating a payment. Your request to the payment system times out, so you don’t know whether the payment succeeded. Meanwhile, the point-of-sale system also times out waiting for you and tells the end-user the transaction failed.

But what if the payment actually succeeded? The end-user may be charged for something they were told they didn’t purchase.

Doing nothing doesn’t always restore the system to a correct state.

Resiliency Requires Correctness

Resiliency isn’t just about making sure something eventually completes. It’s also about maintaining correctness when things fail in unexpected ways.

Sometimes that means retrying. Sometimes it means checking the current state before deciding what to do. And sometimes it requires a compensating action.

  • If a payment fails, maybe you need to cancel a reservation.
  • If a payment outcome is uncertain, maybe you need to put a shipment on hold.
  • If fulfillment fails after the customer was charged, maybe you need to refund the transaction.

These decisions require something a generic retry library, and often a simple AI prompt, doesn’t understand: business context.

Final Thoughts

Retry libraries, exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and infrastructure-level resiliency features are incredibly useful.

But they don’t inherently understand what “correct” means for your business operations. That often requires business logic specifically designed to reconcile or compensate when an outcome is uncertain.

A timeout doesn’t mean an operation failed. It means you don’t know the outcome. Resilient systems need to handle uncertainty.

title: Putin agrees in principle to resume Ukraine peace talks after Nov. 10 as Kyiv urges ceasefire
description:
Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in principle to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine after Nov. 10, following a nearly three-hour meeting on Oct. 21 with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. Kremlin foreign-policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said the technical-level negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and focus on a postwar security framework for Russia and Ukraine. Earlier rounds yielded little progress beyond prisoner exchanges.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supports resuming the talks as soon as possible, preferably by early November, and proposed freezing the current front line as a first step toward a ceasefire. He also called for Ukraine to be included in decisions about its future and said Ukraine’s parliament must approve any peace settlement.

Witkoff brought Putin proposals discussed a day earlier with Zelenskyy and European officials in Oslo, including security guarantees and postwar arrangements. Ushakov said the proposals contained little useful material. Moscow continues to seek terms Kyiv rejects, including Russian control of all of Donetsk and a bar on Ukrainian NATO membership. A technical-level meeting is the next step, but no firm date or venue has been announced. The Kremlin said talks could begin after Nov. 10.

title: UN warns record El Niño could disrupt weather into 2027
description:
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, warned Oct. 21 that the developing El Niño could push sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific to 3.8°C above average from November through January, with a peak around December. The agency said that level would exceed anything in its four decades of monitoring records. El Niño can shift global rainfall patterns, bringing drought to some areas and heavy rain, floods and heat to others.

The WMO expects risks across Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific. Extreme weather has already been reported and could compound humanitarian emergencies. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said about 50 million people could face increased hunger. He said he had released $50 million for 11 countries and called on governments and development finance institutions to fund preparations before damage occurs.

The event is forecast to peak late in 2026, but its effects may persist into 2027 and beyond. Scientists say regional consequences vary: El Niño is a natural climate pattern, but its interaction with human-caused warming and other ocean conditions can influence its effects. Forecasts cannot reliably predict individual storms months in advance.

title: Crocodile relatives tracked warm climates for 250 million years
description:
Crocodile relatives survived climate shifts for roughly 250 million years by following warm conditions across the globe, a study published in Science Advances found. Researchers analyzed more than 7,000 fossils, records from more than 400 extinct and living species, and climate reconstructions spanning 245 million years. They concluded that the animals generally moved toward the poles during warmer periods and retreated toward the equator as temperatures fell.

Climate models of the aftermath of the asteroid impact 66 million years ago showed that tropical and subtropical refuges remained suitable in all but the most extreme scenario tested, in which sunlight fell by 15%. The researchers said climate was not the only factor in survival: smaller body size, semiaquatic habits, flexible diets and low energy needs may also have helped. Study co-author Philip Mannion said modern crocodilians need room to move as the planet warms, while roads, farms and cities are reducing suitable habitat.

Lost diversity: Crocodile relatives known as pseudosuchians included land predators, armored plant-eaters, marine forms and filter-feeders, far beyond the ecological range of living crocodilians (reuters.com, aawsat.com).

title: Macron rebukes Trump over France riots as Paris bans protests
description:
French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday accused US President Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of exploiting France’s unrest for electoral gain after Trump blamed the violence on migrants, jihadists and communists. Macron said he saw no evidence of foreign interference in the unrest itself, but said misleading information, including AI-generated images of scenes that did not occur in France, had circulated afterward.

The unrest began with student demonstrations over school conditions and grew to include protests over living costs. On Oct. 17, violence, looting and clashes with police followed mass protests in cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon. The government acknowledged it had lost control of the violence, and more than 2,000 people were detained.

Paris police banned demonstrations on Thursday in parts of the capital, including near the presidential palace, parliament, the Louvre and the Champs-Elysees. Authorities were preparing to reinforce security for protests planned for Saturday, Oct. 24, while Macron was due to meet ministers and intelligence officials for a detailed account of the unrest.

title: The Surprising Origins of Native Hawaiians
description:
Hawaii is one of the most isolated islands on Earth, surrounded by vast oceans for thousands of miles on every side. And yet humans have been living there for nearly a millennia. They’re part of the Polynesian diaspora. This culture of ultravoyagers embarked on their own age of exploration while Europe was still mired in the Middle Ages, colonizing the tiny islands dotting the South Pacific without the benefit of metal tools, navigational equipment, or a written language. Now, a new study published in Science Advances is better defining their genetic history. 

“What we uncover in this paper is where the Native people of Hawaii had come from,” study author Alexander Ioannidis of Stanford University said in a statement. “Hawaii is the only Polynesian island in the Northern Hemisphere, so it’s a long way from everything.”

Read more: “Hawaii’s False Killer Whales Are Wasting Away”

title: Meta faces $25 billion New Mexico penalty as legal costs cut earnings
description:
Meta reported third-quarter operating income of $13 billion, down 37% from a year earlier, after a $9.9 billion charge for a separate youth-safety settlement. The same day, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion in a privacy case. Meta’s revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, and the company attributed advertising gains in part to artificial intelligence improvements in engagement and recommendations.

The New Mexico order followed a jury’s finding that Meta committed more than 43 million state consumer-protection violations. The judge calculated a potential penalty of more than $219 billion before reducing it to $25 billion. Interest on the award accrues at 15% annually, and the state’s constitution directs consumer-protection penalties to education spending.

Meta says it will appeal, a step expected to delay access to the money. Its shares rose 2% in Wednesday afternoon trading, and an analyst quoted by Reuters said the award was unlikely to change the company’s overall value.

title: Russia frees detained American Stephen Hubbard during Ukraine peace talks
description:
Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American jailed for more than four years, during U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff’s meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. title: Full-scale wave test shows salt marshes can buffer coastal storms
description:
Researchers moved 306 square meters of intact salt marsh into the Delta Flume, a large wave-testing facility in Delft, Netherlands, and exposed it to waves as high as 2 meters. After 21 hours, the marsh surface had eroded by an average of just 7 millimeters, while its vegetation suffered progressive damage.

The study found that plants can reduce wave energy by more than 10%, and by as much as 50% on lower-energy coasts with waves up to 1 meter. Their effect declines as waves grow higher and vegetation is lost. Researchers say marshes could work alongside dikes and seawalls, not replace them. A Spanish coastal-engineering expert questioned how well the Dutch experiment applies to other coastlines, citing wave periods and mobile seabeds among other factors.

title: U.S. emissions rise worsens global warming outlook, UN report says
description:
The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 emissions assessment says U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 133 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2025, the largest increase among major economies. The United States accounted for about 70% of the net increase among 124 countries whose emissions grew. The report warns that the world can no longer avoid exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C threshold and must limit the overshoot.

The U.S. increase reflected higher electricity demand and a rebound in coal-fired power generation, while global greenhouse-gas emissions remained roughly level at 58.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The assessment attributes its worsening projections partly to the United States’ formal withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions.

Under existing policies, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; fully meeting national climate pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. UNEP says a pathway offering about a 50% chance of limiting peak warming to 1.7–1.8°C and returning to 1.5°C by 2100 requires global emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025. The next UN climate summit, COP31, is scheduled to open in Antalya, Türkiye, next month.

title: What 32,000 Folds Did to the iPhone Duo's Hinge
description:
Apple hasn't shared iPhone Duo hinge tests or given a lifetime fold number like Samsung, but Joanna Stern used a custom device to subject her review unit to more than 32,000 folds over four nights.


Over the course of the testing, Stern said she thought it might be feeling looser as the number of folds increased, but her final conclusion was that she couldn't feel much of a change. A calibrated push-pull gauge used to take readings before and after the Duo fold test showed the hinge was actually stiffer than before.
But in everyday use, I really couldn't feel a difference. So, after 32,000 folds, it felt pretty much the same as day one, which is pretty darn impressive.

Stern didn't comment on whether the fold test caused the crease to be more visible, which can happen over time with other foldable devices. Her testing was done with a case on, and while the machine opened the Duo flat, it didn't close it all the way each time.


Samsung's foldable displays undergo official testing, and in 2025, the display used for the Galaxy Z Fold7 passed a 500,000-fold durability test. Samsung Display says that translates to over 10 years for average users folding their device about 100 times a day, or over six years for users who fold it more than 200 times daily.

Until Apple shares information on display and hinge durability, Stern's test is all we have to go on. It's unlikely to be the last unofficial folding stress test that we see over the next few weeks.

The full details on Stern's machine, including how it was built, can be found in her YouTube video, and she has more information in her review writeup.

title: Smith tells UCP separatists to accept referendum result or leave the party
description:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Wednesday told separatists to stop publicly advocating for independence or leave her United Conservative Party (UCP), after voters rejected moving toward a binding separation referendum by roughly three to one. The nonbinding Oct. 19 referendum also asked about immigration and constitutional changes. Preliminary results showed majorities for eight of the other nine proposals.

Smith said people may hold their own views, but UCP candidates, provincial board members and constituency association representatives must support “a strong Alberta within a united Canada.” She warned that a year of internal division could cost the party the provincial election, scheduled for October 2027.

Separatist organizers say they will seek influence inside the party rather than form a new one. They are organizing for the UCP’s annual meeting, which opens Nov. 27, where delegates elect board members and set party policy. Smith has not detailed how she will enforce the new rules.

title: AI models uncover decades-old PHP flaws, heightening cyberattack risks
description:
Researchers at cybersecurity firm Calif used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model to find a critical flaw in PHP. Google-owned security company Wiz independently used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI models to identify vulnerabilities in the same core software. PHP maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for the two flaws, which had remained hidden for years and could let attackers run code on vulnerable servers without authentication.

Wiz said frontier models made a complex exploit chain substantially easier to execute, describing steps that had once been at the edge of what human researchers could achieve. The same capabilities could help attackers adapt exploits to different PHP versions and server configurations, the company warned.

OpenAI said it believes researchers found the flaws before attackers did. It is proposing a repeatable process for identifying and fixing vulnerabilities in widely used software and preparing defenses against them. The company said it expects similar discoveries to increase sharply in coming months.

Wiz said frontier models made a complex exploit chain substantially easier to execute, describing steps that had once been at the edge of what human researchers could achieve (wiz.io). The same capabilities could help attackers adapt exploits to different PHP versions and server configurations, the company warned (techcrunch.com, axios.com). OpenAI said it believes researchers found the flaws before attackers did. It is proposing a repeatable process for identifying and fixing vulnerabilities in widely used software and preparing defenses against them. The company said it expects similar discoveries to increase sharply in coming months (openai.com). Vulnerability surge: A graph compiled by research nonprofit Epoch AI showed significant vulnerabilities reported by major technology companies and open-source projects rising from a few dozen in some months several years ago to about 600 in a typical month (motherjones.com). OpenAI funding: OpenAI pledged $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access for frontline defenders, with a focus on organizations that have limited security resources (openai.com). Exposure checker: OpenAI published a PHP version-checking tool as a Codex skill to help operators identify potentially vulnerable installations and determine relevant updates (openai.com). Proof-of-concept video: An accidentally posted video showed an exploit working against multiple targets; copies spread online and contributed to faster development and circulation of exploit demonstrations (simonwillison.net).

title: Attackers compromise AI gateway LiteLLM 1.107.0 to steal credentials
description:
Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM.

LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues.

The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service
excerpt: Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM (thehackernews.com, safedep.io, theregister.com). LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues (thehackernews.com, ithome.com.tw, safedep.io). Build integrity: SafeDep, which analyzed the compromised package, found that the public v1.107.0 GitHub tag did not contain the payload. An added data = "cook" line in the source distribution’s pyproject.toml caused payload files to be included in the wheels (safedep.io). Image tags: The compromised Docker images included the floating tags latest, main-latest and main-stable, so users could pull them without explicitly requesting version 1.107.0 (reddit.com, safedep.io, ithome.com.tw). Data exposure: The stealer could extract stored provider keys from LiteLLM proxy database tables when a database connection was available, in addition to credentials held elsewhere on the host (safedep.io, reddit.com). Scale and warning: LiteLLM receives about 23 million weekly downloads. Security researchers urged teams to investigate any host or continuous integration (CI) runner where Python ran after installation (theregister.com).

title: Google adds Gemini scam detection and ClickFix warnings to Chrome
description:
Google has added new scam defenses to Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode, a higher-security setting in its Safe Browsing service: warnings for suspicious sites, expanded Gemini-powered scam detection and alerts when users copy potentially malicious commands. The new site warning uses a less severe alert for deceptive patterns detected with lower confidence; sites deemed dangerous still trigger Chrome’s full-screen red warning. A server-side Gemini model expands detection to fake antivirus and browser-update scams, beyond the tech-support scams targeted by Chrome’s earlier on-device model.

The command warning targets ClickFix, a social-engineering tactic that persuades people to copy and run commands under the pretext of fixing a computer problem. Chrome removes personal information from a suspected command before sending it to Safe Browsing for analysis, then warns if Safe Browsing judges the command dangerous. Google says it sends page text for Gemini analysis only when a site shows strong scam indicators and does not log, retain or use that text to train models.

Chrome has also enabled prompts for all users before connecting to unencrypted HTTP sites. The prompt appears on a first visit, and Chrome will not show it again until a user has gone at least two weeks without visiting that site.

title: AI-discovered PHP flaws prompt global website shutdowns as patches roll out
description:
PHP’s maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical vulnerabilities that could let attackers run code on exposed web servers without logging in, prompting governments and companies to take websites offline while they applied patches. The flaws, rated 9.2 out of 10, affect PHP installations serving web requests; the PHP team released patched versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12.

Precautionary shutdowns affected public services and businesses in Europe, Australia and Asia. France disabled local-government sites, the Netherlands took its DigiD digital identity portal and parliamentary sites offline, and Japanese companies suspended some online services; Wikipedia’s operator also temporarily took supporting systems offline. PHP underpins an estimated 70% of websites, though only sites running PHP on their own servers are exposed.

Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws using AI tools in August, and details leaked online on Oct. 20, a day before the planned patch release. Cloudflare reported millions of exploitation attempts after disclosure, while Amazon said it detected an attempt against a decoy system on Oct. 17; reports described attempts but no confirmed successful exploitation at that point. Agencies advised organizations to patch promptly or isolate vulnerable systems until they could apply the fixes.

title: Stanford team revives bleached corals through brief clone contact
description:
Stanford researchers report that bleached coral fragments fully recovered within seven weeks in laboratory tests after brief contact with healthy, genetically identical clones, according to a study published Oct. 14 in *Science Advances*. Contact lasting five days to a week was sometimes enough; bleached fragments kept a few millimeters away from healthy partners died.

Microscopic channels in the corals’ tissues aligned, allowing beneficial algae to move between fragments within three days. Inside bleached fragments, algae populations doubled every four days during the second week. The method requires matching clones, limiting its use across reefs. The researchers plan to test other ways to deliver algae, including collecting it from healthy corals before heat waves.

title: AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds
description:
AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere Labs found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a staff research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

title: The UN’s latest climate change report is spotlighting the U.S., and not for a good reason
description:
Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says.

If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.

“This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report.

The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries’ climate fighting plans. He wasn’t part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound.

Shooting far past Paris climate goal

The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection.

Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees.

The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.”

Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen.

“The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn’t part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.”

An added tenth of a degree of danger

Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century.

“This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.”

Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rain forest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann.

And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming other nations ease off in their efforts too, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany.

“The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

title: UK approves Jackdaw gas field despite acknowledged risk to climate leadership
description:
The UK government approved gas production at the Jackdaw field in the North Sea on Oct. 21, while its own decision document acknowledged the move could weaken Britain’s climate leadership and make it harder to persuade other countries to stop producing fossil fuels. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh gave that concern “moderate negative weight” against the project’s claimed benefits, saying the approval remained compatible with the UK’s climate targets and 2050 net-zero goal.

The UK experienced record heat, drought and wildfires this summer. The United Nations has said global emissions must fall by nearly one-fifth over the next four years to limit climate damage. Campaigners argue Jackdaw will add emissions without materially lowering household bills; government supporters say domestically produced gas can displace higher-emission imports.

Legal scholar Margaretha Wewerinke-Singh, who led Vanuatu’s legal team pushing for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) climate advisory opinion, said the government’s treatment of its climate obligations misstates international law. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to represent the UK at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya next month.

title: PHP patches two critical flaws enabling unauthenticated server takeover
description:
The PHP project released emergency fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical flaws that can let unauthenticated attackers run code remotely on servers processing PHP requests. The vulnerabilities, rated 9.2 out of 10, affect PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11; fixes are available in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12.

PHP also runs in appliances and network devices, and a working exploit against Apache mod_php can trigger before application code executes. Google is rolling out updates to supported serverless PHP runtimes, but customers using custom containers, unsupported runtimes or self-managed installations must arrange upgrades and redeploy or restart affected services.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said it had not observed exploitation as of Wednesday afternoon. Amazon Threat Intelligence later reported that its MadPot honeypot had recorded an attempt on Oct. 17, before public disclosure. How the actor obtained exploit details remains unknown. Security agencies urged organizations unable to patch promptly to isolate exposed systems, and administrators were advised to check for signs of compromise as well as install fixes.

title: Carney and Ford commit $8.7 billion to tariff-hit Ontario industries
description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced an $8.7-billion federal-provincial package on Oct. 21 for Ontario’s steel and auto industries and roads to the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region. The plan allocates about $5.2 billion to steel over five years, $2.5 billion to autos over two years and up to $1 billion in federal funding for roads over three years, matching Ontario’s contribution.

The governments say the investments will help mills modernize, support auto production and reduce reliance on U.S. markets as tariffs disrupt trade. The package also includes stronger enforcement against steel dumping, a joint steel task force and a coordinated process for mine permits. A working group will engage First Nations on economic development and conservation, including possible Indigenous protected areas.

title: AI developer Anthropic pitches draft bill limiting federal power over models
description:
Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI assistant, has circulated a draft bill limiting when the U.S. Commerce Department could seek a court order to halt an advanced AI model. The model would have to pose a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or more than $1 billion in damage. The threat would have to involve a cyberattack, a model evading its developer’s controls, or the creation or release of a biological weapon. A federal judge would decide whether to block the model.

The proposal would bar other federal agencies from independently suspending a model. Registered independent evaluators could assess companies and models, and labs could pay them as long as payment did not depend on their findings. Evaluators would have 72 hours to report a qualifying imminent risk to Commerce.

Critics say the high thresholds and court requirement constrain regulators, while Anthropic says its approach would allow intervention against dangerous models. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei defended the company’s safety record, arguing that it must stay at the frontier to influence industry standards. Anthropic has said it will revise parts of the draft, including its language on preempting state rules, and develop evaluator requirements.

title: UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
description:
The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025.

The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C.

The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

excerpt: The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans (wxyz.com, rte.ie). Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9 (un.org, arynews.tv). Methane target: The pathway calls for methane emissions to fall at least 25% by 2035 (wxyz.com). Carbon removal: Returning to 1.5°C after an overshoot would require removing and permanently storing about 320 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide this century; UNEP notes substantial uncertainty about whether that scale can be achieved (rte.ie). U.S. policy effect: The report estimates U.S. emissions in 2030 will be nearly 0.9 gigatonnes higher than projections based on policies under the Biden administration (gizmodo.com). Renewables growth: Since the 2015 Paris Agreement, global renewable electricity capacity has expanded three times faster than anticipated, while solar photovoltaic capacity grew seven times faster (pbl.nl). Delay penalty: Every five years of CO₂ emissions at current levels would add about 0.1°C to peak warming (rte.ie).

title: Canadian firearms panel has yet to meet as SKS review awaits advice
description:
Canada’s federal firearms-classification advisory group has not met nearly a year after Ottawa announced a review that includes the SKS rifle. The group, which will advise Public Safety Canada and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, is expected to hold its first meeting later this fall. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the government will consider the group’s advice before deciding the SKS’s status. The RCMP has not disclosed which firearms were used in the Feb. 10 Tumbler Ridge shooting, in which 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people before taking her own life.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the review would include consultations with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities. Gun-control group PolySeSouvient is calling for restrictions on SKS sales and a voluntary buyback, with an exemption for Indigenous subsistence hunters. The Canadian Shooting Sports Association says key questions about the shooting remain unanswered.

Opposing view: The Canadian Shooting Sports Association argues that reclassifying a firearm before authorities clarify which guns were used or how they were obtained would not show that a ban could have prevented the shooting (globalnews.ca, nationalobserver.com).

title: Google Cloud outage disrupts European banks as regulators seek answers
description:
Google Cloud, Google’s cloud-computing service, restored operations after a power-related outage in its London europe-west2 region disrupted Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC, along with other online services, on Oct. 20. The outage lasted 7 hours and 52 minutes and was centered on the europe-west2-b availability zone. Google attributed it to a power event at a third-party facility.

The European Banking Authority (EBA), the EU banking regulator, contacted Google to assess the effects on financial institutions, while Britain’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it was engaging with the company. Parliament’s Treasury Committee sought details from the Bank of England and FCA about the disruption’s scale and any financial harm. Google said it would publish an analysis on its public status dashboard.

excerpt: Google Cloud, Google’s cloud-computing service, restored operations after a power-related outage in its London europe-west2 region disrupted Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC, along with other online services, on Oct. 20. The outage lasted 7 hours and 52 minutes and was centered on the europe-west2-b availability zone. Google attributed it to a power event at a third-party facility (reuters.com, techrepublic.com). The European Banking Authority (EBA), the EU banking regulator, contacted Google to assess the effects on financial institutions, while Britain’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it was engaging with the company. Services affected: The outage disrupted Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage; Google said Looker Studio was unaffected (techrepublic.com). Banking functions: Revolut customers reported problems with logins, card payments and cash withdrawals; reports also described issues with transfers, currency exchange and securities transactions (reuters.com, mixnews.lv). Wider disruption: Reports described disruptions at delivery companies DPD and Royal Mail, property site Rightmove and remote court hearings using a videoconferencing platform (cafe-dc.com, mixnews.lv). Regulatory rules: Under Britain’s critical third-party provider regime, Google Cloud must report serious outages to the FCA and Bank of England (reuters.com).

title: UK inflation and borrowing exceed forecasts ahead of Healey’s Budget
description:
UK inflation accelerated as the Iran war drove fuel costs higher, while government borrowing also exceeded forecasts ahead of Finance Minister John Healey’s first Budget. Consumer prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and above economists’ forecast of 3.4%. The rate was the highest since October 2025.

Motor fuels were the biggest contributor to the rise: prices rose 29.8% year over year, while services inflation reached 3.7% and core inflation rose to 2.8%. Food inflation held at 1.3%. Separately, the government borrowed £24.5 billion in September, £1.8 billion more than a year earlier, and public debt topped £3 trillion. Borrowing from April to September reached £97.8 billion, £6 billion above the fiscal watchdog’s forecast.

Healey will present his Budget on Oct. 28. The September inflation reading determines increases in several benefits next April. Investors expect the Bank of England to raise its benchmark interest rate from 3.75% to 4% at its Nov. 5 meeting, though no increase has yet been announced.

title: Impermanence by Design: An Architectural History of Antarctica
description: "Antarctica is known through narratives," states Victoria Nuviala Antelo during the lecture on Inhabiting the Extreme: An Architectural Biography of Antarctica, presented at the Buenos Aires International Architecture Biennial. Indeed, throughout architectural history, numerous stories, experiences, ways of inhabiting, and building practices have often been excluded from official narratives. Buried beneath thick layers of ice, the history of Antarctic architecture tells a story of impermanence. The ice surrounding the continent expands and contracts each year, doubling its surface area, while the species that inhabit it migrate and return according to their life cycles. Ice covers structures as katabatic winds erase the traces of more than 200 years of human presence. Explorations, settlements, architectural interventions, and ways of inhabiting remain concealed within one of the most extreme landscapes on the planet.

A big band in the Williams Lake might seem a bit unusual but the Cariboo Gold Dance Band (CGDB) has been playing together for over 42 years. This 14-piece band, comprised of skilled and dedicated local musicians, played its first dance in the spring of 1984 and has performed for a wide variety of occasions in the Cariboo and beyond ever since. Each year the band brings to the community a professional to work with the CGDB and then perform as a featured artist. This year the dance band will be hosting the triple Juno award recipient and internationally respected saxophone player, Campbell Ryga. Anyone who has enjoyed the music of Michael Bublé and his Grammy winning album, _Crazy Love_, would have heard Campbell’s skillful sax playing. He has also been featured on over 87 other jazz recordings, often as a leader. Most notably, Campbell Ryga is a founding member of the award-winning Hugh Fraser Quintet. British Columbia is full of international acclaimed jazz musicians and Campbell Ryga is no exception. He was born in 1961 in Edmonton but was raised in Summerland, and is the eldest son of renowned author and playwright George Ryga. When he was 18, Ryga moved to Vancouver to pursue advanced musical studies. He has since lived and worked in Vancouver, Toronto, and New York City, establishing an international reputation as both a band leader and creative jazz artist. Ryga is currently based in Kelowna, and serves as a clinician, adjudicator, arts juror and it is a natural fit for him to be the headline performer in the Cariboo Gold Dance Band’s upcoming concert on Saturday, Nov. 14. title: ‘This petrol station is my home now’: Malawi’s fuel crisis forces desperate drivers to queue for days
description:
Shortages caused by the country’s lack of hard currency have escalated into a national emergency, with drivers waiting for a fuel tanker that may never arrive

From the driver’s seat of his rusted minibus, Sido Sombeja stares out at a stationary sea of rear lights stretching for almost a mile down the road. It is 3am in Zomba, the old capital of Malawi, and cold night air comes through the cracked windscreen. For eight consecutive days and nights, the 40-year-old father of four has lived out of this vehicle, waiting for a fuel tanker that may never arrive.

Sombeja chews on a cold piece of fried mandazi – a doughy snack that has been the only food available. The Meru petrol station is no longer just a place of transit; it has transformed into a makeshift village of drivers in parked vehicles. In these queues, strangers form uneasy alliances. Motorists group together to guard one another’s vehicles during rare bathroom breaks, and coordinate to aggressively block any queue-jumpers. Men sleep under the bellies of trucks. They wash their faces with bottled water on the kerbside and gather around charcoal braziers (mbaula) at night.

Field tour participants review an area affected by a 2022 wildfire, shown in pink on the map, on a tour with the Kaslo and District Community Forest. British Columbia’s (B.C.) forest sector is at a turning point. Communities are feeling the effects of sawmill and pulp mill closures, catastrophic wildfires, changing markets, and general uncertainty about the future. British Columbians are also asking how forests can support healthy ecosystems, sustainable local economies, reconciliation, public safety, recreation, and other community priorities. We believe community forestry offers a tested and proven way forward and should be on the minds of British Columbians and on the platforms of those running for office in the provincial election. Community forests put decisions about local forests closer to the people who understand those places and live with the outcomes. Through long-term community forest agreements, a range of local organizations—including municipalities, First Nations, community organizations, and partnerships—can manage nearby forests according to local values. And the good news? The community forest model is already working across B.C. There are 62 operating community forests, each shaped by their local landscape, economy, relationships, and priorities. More than half are held directly by First Nations or operated through partnerships involving First Nations, creating opportunities for shared stewardship, economic participation, and reconciliation. Each community forest is unique, but they share the same fundamental goals, including responsible local stewardship, economic benefits that remain in the community, and sustainable management for future generations. Greens Leader Emily Lowan, CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, B.C. Conservatives
excerpt: Where the parties stand on the major issues heading into the B.C. election | Williams Lake Tribune Where the parties stand on the major issues heading into the B.C. election B.C. provincial party leaders from left: B.C. Greens Leader Emily Lowan, CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, B.C. Conservatives Leader Lorne Doerkson, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby and OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie. Amid the avalanche of policy announcements, platform promises and attack ads, it can be hard to know where party leaders really stand on the issues. Mario Canseco of Research Co. regularly polls British Columbian voters to ask which issues they care most about. For the past three years, housing has led. This year, it is cost-of-living. In a poll conducted on Oct. 13, the economy/jobs was the top issue for 25 per cent of respondents; housing/poverty/homelessness for 23 per cent; healthcare for 21 per cent, and crime/public safety for nine per cent. With the cost of living the top issue for most voters, economic concerns moved to the forefront as the campaigns hit the home stretch. A back-and-forth emerged as campaigns questioned each other’s math and whether spending or tax-cut promises are realistic. After 10 years in power, the NDP is defending its economic record amid historic deficits. The party’s main new plank is a proposed income tax hike on the wealthiest 3.88 per cent of British Columbians.
