title: Perplexity Computer Can Now Run Fully Locally on Mac
description:
Perplexity today said it is updating Perplexity Computer to run fully locally on Mac. The local version runs on Qwen 3.6 or PPLX Pro (a post-trained version of Qwen) in the Perplexity app for Mac on supported Apple silicon Macs.


Perplexity highlights the new Mac mini machines and says 36GB of memory or more is recommended to run locally. With the local setup, the AI model, task planning, reasoning, and file processing are handled on-device. Code and tool execution run in isolated sandbox environments.

Computer can use native apps on the Mac and complete tasks without sending personal data to the cloud. Perplexity says it can work across apps like Notes, Messages, Mail, Keynote, and Numbers.

Perplexity also offers Hybrid Compute, which combines frontier models that run in the cloud with local models to process information privately. It's an alternative for users who want local processing but don't have a Mac that's powerful enough. Hybrid Compute works on Macs with as little as 24GB of memory,

When running Computer locally, if a task requires current information, browser use, or cloud-connected apps, users can authorize cloud access and decide when to spend credits. There's also an option to call on one of more than 15 frontier models for tougher problems when needed.

Local Computer for Mac is available now for Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. Users can download Perplexity for Mac and then choose the fully local option to use it.

Sam Roberts Band and Owen Riegling are this year’s performers on the CPKC Holiday Train as it makes its way across Alberta and British Columbia this December. This is the 28th year for the holiday event which sees two trains – one which travels a predominantly Canadian route and the other mostly in the U.S. – making stops in different communities to offer free concerts, and raise money and collect non-perishable food items for food banks across North America. Cars on each of the trains are lit up in brightly coloured Christmas-themed displays. The U.S. Holiday Train kicks off on Nov. 19, in Montreal, and will wind south through towns across the United States, before traveling north again into Saskatchewan, where it will make its final stop. The Canadian Holiday Train kicks off on Nov. 21 in Jackman, Maine, in the United States, and will make its way west, through Quebec, down to New York, back into Ontario, then Manitoba, and into Saskatchewan, and then Alberta and B.C. “We are so proud to be part of the CPKC Holiday Train once again,” said the Sam Roberts Band online, noting it has been eight years since they last performed on the Holiday Train. Or, as they put it, “last rode the rails and rocked the mountains with you all, and we are very excited to do it all over.” From Calgary to Banff in Alberta and then from Golden, all the way to the final stop in Port Coquitlam, the band will be playing 33 shows from Dec. 11 to 20. title: 1865 St. Francis Canoe Launched
description:
Back in September, I wrote that I hadn’t seen any replicas built of the 1865 St. Francis 2-Fathom Canoe, which appears as Figure 80 in The Bark Canoes and Skin Boats of North America, until Evan B. sent me photos of his 1865 St. Francis Canoe build. Now, we have another cedar-strip replica built and on the water. Ph. Payen sent a few photos of his new canoe. He wrote: Please find herewith a couple of pictures of a 1865 St Francis canoe made out of white pine, a tad heavy (62 pounds). I left the plywood apron inside stem and stern, and covered them with fiberglass to make watertight compartments. Gunwales had to be steamed, but the result is worth it. I used it solo to this day, and I am not certain my wife will join me one day. We are absolute beginners in paddling, and I must admit that the first trials were quite wet. There does not seem to be any kind of secondary stability, but it moves effortlessly, and it is a very pleasant way to be on the water. When I made my 3D model based on the drawings in The Bark Canoes and Skin Boats of North America, I I couldn’t find any photos before I released the free canoe plans. Now we have two builders within months showing off their builds. That’s amazing. Thanks to Ph. Payen for sending these over. The canoe looks amazing!

The post 1865 St. Francis Canoe Launched appeared first on PaddlingLight.com. You can leave a comment by clicking here: 1865 St. Francis Canoe Launched.

title: U.S. bans AI startup DeepSeek because of ‘threat vectors’ and China responds
description:
China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products for federal civilian agencies, highlighting friction in the two AI powers’ heated technology race.

The agencies should remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, the Department of Homeland Security said in a notice made public on Monday.

The department’s order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. DeepSeek is one of China’s leading and best-known AI companies and its open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States. They are mostly free to use.

The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” It said concerns include that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities’ could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data.

In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China will “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked at a regular press conference about the U.S. ban.

“China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues,” she told reporters at a routine briefing.

DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC, or Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China.

AI is expected to be on the agenda.

China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up of a notification system on national security-related incidents, but the two countries are still at odds on many issues.

U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them. Last week, Beijing rolled out new proposed plans to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.

The U.S. has also said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced it was barring imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots in a move seen as targeting China.

—Chan Ho-Him, AP Business Writer

title: Alberta First Nations report voting barriers in provincial referendum
description:
First Nations leaders in Alberta say ballot shortages, late-opening polling stations and identification rules obstructed some Indigenous voters during Monday’s provincial referendum. The nonbinding vote asked whether Alberta should begin legal steps toward a future separation referendum; about three-quarters of voters chose to remain in Canada, and Premier Danielle Smith said she would not call another separation vote while she is premier [aptnnews.ca#1][cbc.ca#5][thestar.com#1].

Treaty 8 campaign manager Jay Telegdi said he received reports of voters turned away because of identification and polling problems. Elections Alberta said it delivered extra ballots to five First Nations communities, three of which received multiple deliveries. The agency said 36 First Nations communities participated, up from 33 in 2023 [cbc.ca#5][theglobeandmail.com#11]. Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot called for changes to prevent similar barriers in future elections [aptnnews.ca#3].

The count on the nine other ballot questions remained unsettled Tuesday. Preliminary results showed support for all five immigration proposals and close contests on constitutional measures; Smith said she would pursue immigration reforms in the months and years ahead. Elections Alberta scheduled the official results for Oct. 29 [lethbridgeherald.com#3][timescolonist.com#2][cbc.ca#3].

title: New details emerge on former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a conference room
description:
A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.

Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, traveling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention.

“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”

A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov.

Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” — U.S. citizenship.

Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said.

Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets — about $1 million currently in a U.S. investment account — to cover his bond.

“Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033.

Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond.

After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment.

Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.

But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked.

Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.

Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest.

Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.

Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”

OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.

—Barbara Ortutay and Philip Marcelo, Associated Press

This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

title: ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
description:
Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.

The Social Planning Council continues to work on making a difference in Williams Lake and area through its poverty reduction strategy. At the latest regular city council meeting this month, Angelika Sellick presented an update on the Thrive Poverty Reduction Strategy and the work of the Poverty Reduction Working Group. The working group was formed in 2018 with the strategy that was endorsed by city council published in 2021 following extensive community consultation. “We all know the social planning council is in no way the only organization that is doing poverty reduction work in our community,” Sellick acknowledged, adding they recognize and celebrate the richness of organizations doing poverty reduction in their own communities without any direct connection to the Social Planning Council established in 1995. Through community consultation Sellick said the Social Planning Council has come to understand poverty as the condition in which people lack the resources, means, choices and opportunities to maintain self-sufficiency and a quality of life that supports basic needs, dignity and meaningful participation in the community. The Social Planning Council is a table that meets monthly to learn, share and collaborate on practical action and advocacy leading to increased community social well-being. Some organizations involved are the Salvation Army, Interior Health, Gibraltar Mine, the Foundry Cariboo Chilcotin, Women’s Contact Society, and WorkBC, in addition to representatives from city council. “Poverty is not the outcome of personal deficiencies or lack of will. It is the result of greater systemic failures,” Sellick said further noting poverty reduction work at the local level can contribute and lead to the ending of poverty at a global level. Ross Hickey, an associate professor of economics and management at UBC Okanagan, says this type of growth is unlikely. He gave a “cautiously optimistic” forecast of one per cent GDP growth per year for the next three years. The Bank of Canada projects national GDP growth at 0.7 per cent this year, 1.8 per cent next year, and 1.8 per cent the year after that. The Royal Bank of Canada projects B.C.’s economy to grow 0.8 per cent this year and 1.5 per cent next year. title: ‘From actually doing work’ to ‘babysitting Claudes’: Anthropic employees on how their jobs have changed in the past year
description:
What’s it really like to work at Anthropic? The AI company made headlines last month when an employee resigned, claiming the company is “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” and that conversations about an AI-powered doomsday are par for the course among staff.

Now Anthropic is pulling back the curtain on its own workplace with a new report on the impact of AI adoption at the company.

Anthropic says its internal trends “could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.” If it’s right, that means a world with fewer entry-level jobs, new roadblocks to productivity, and a workforce full of babysitters for AI agents.

The babysitters club

Anthropic reports that AI is responsible for massive booms in productivity, saying its internal use of Claude tools has led to “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.”

Its AI tools are so productive, in fact, that Anthropic now says human interference is responsible for bottlenecks in productivity. AI agents at the company spend 80% of their session time waiting for human input rather than actively working.

Though employees agree that using Claude tools improves their productivity, they say it also shifts their day-to-day responsibilities—and not always for the better.

In an April 2026 survey, 75% of Anthropic employees said they believe the company’s work processes make them productive. Responding to an open-ended question about how AI impacts their daily routines, 20% said their roles have shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes,” a task that one employee said is equivalent to babysitting children who can’t accurately gauge the importance of different tasks and problems.

“They’re like, ‘I need my juice box opened and it’s an emergency that my juice box is opened.’ And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding,” the employee said. “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Another employee said there’s an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything,” while a third of all employees reported that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.”

When they’re not babysitting agents, the Anthropic staff’s time is also increasingly spent in meetings. The median employee spends 20% more time in meetings compared to a year ago: “A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting,” reads the report, adding that interviewed employees describe “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

A more senior team

As more and more work is delegated to AI agents, Anthropic’s hiring needs and practices are shifting to match. 

That means making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior hires in Anthropic’s technical departments falling from 27% to just 9% since early 2025. The overall share of junior-level technical employees also fell in the same window, shrinking from 21% to 14%.

Anthropic attributes this reduced demand for junior hires to teams offloading work to Claude, including writing code and finding bugs. AI agents at the company now work far longer hours than humans do, with interactive AI agents logging six times as many hours as human employees as of August.

title: AI expertise isn’t the same as AI oversight. Boards need both
description:
From 2023 to 2025, the share of S&P 500 companies disclosing AI as a risk jumped from 12% to 83%. But according to company filings, fewer than 3% of directors have AI expertise. And in the same research, just 23% of executives said their board was highly fluent in AI, and a quarter said their board had low fluency or none at all. As artificial intelligence spreads across the business, that leaves a significant gap between what boards understand and what they are required to oversee.

That gap is untenable—and this is what boards need to do to fill it.


Expertise is necessary but insufficient

If the problem is that boards lack AI expertise, the obvious answer is to recruit directors who have it. Well, yes, but not quite. Boards do need more AI experts, but recruiting experts is not enough to close the gap. There are two reasons for this.

First, AI isn’t siloed. It runs through hiring, pricing, customer service, credit, and operations. There is no single AI agenda item for one expert to own, and every director will vote on matters AI has shaped, whether they realize it or not. Oversight must therefore be distributed across the board, not concentrated in a limited number of expert seats.

Second, expertise is not the same thing as competent oversight. Expertise is what you know about AI; oversight is what you do about it as a director. Expertise is often needed for competent oversight, but it doesn’t guarantee it. For instance, someone can understand exactly how a large language model works without ever asking who in the company is accountable for one, or what an AI agent is allowed to spend.

So boards face two questions about AI. The first is whether the board knows enough. The second is whether each director is competent at oversight. Answering the first doesn’t answer the second—and while everyone focuses on the first, the second is largely neglected.

What the board needs to oversee: The key areas of AI oversight

Before we figure out what competent oversight involves, we need to be clear about what directors are meant to be overseeing. The following areas, drawn from our ongoing research into how directors oversee AI, are foundational. Each of these is a place where AI can do real damage to a company, and a board that covers some of them but not the others is dangerously exposed.

  • Governance Oversight: Knowing which individual is accountable for each AI matter, and making sure that they are actually held accountable.
  • Data Inquiry: Knowing what data the company’s AI uses, where it goes, and on what legal basis. This must be backed by evidence rather than a vendor’s assurance.
  • Explanation & Disclosure: Making sure the company can explain an AI decision to the person it was made about, and that its public claims about AI match what it does.
  • Fairness & Affected Parties: Knowing which groups a system could disadvantage, when it was last tested, and whether problems were fixed rather than just recorded.
  • Risk & Irreversibility: Knowing what the company’s AI can do that cannot be undone, and how the board would hear about a failure.
  • Human Judgment & Workforce: Making sure a person can overrule a system in practice, not just on paper, and that the people whose work AI changes are part of the plan.
  • Autonomy & Agent Authority: Knowing what AI agents may do, spend, and commit on their own, and making sure each one has a limit and a way to stop it.

That is what a board needs to oversee. But how do you actually build competent oversight of those areas? Three principles help you get there.

Measure what people do—not what they know

The strongest possible evidence for being able to perform a task is that you regularly perform it to a high standard.

Therefore, rather than only asking if your directors understand AI oversight at a theoretical level, you also need to ask: Have you actually performed this basic task of AI oversight recently? How often? Is it something that is a systematic part of your oversight process?

The point is that being aware of something is not the same as doing it, let alone being good at doing it. In PwC’s 2025 survey of public company directors, two-thirds said their board should spend more time on AI, but fewer than half said their board had an approach to actually overseeing it.

For example, almost every director would agree that the board should know which AI systems the company uses. Far fewer have actually asked to see the list, and fewer still ask for it every time the board reviews AI risk.

First Step: Ask each director to name the last AI oversight act they performed, and when and where it happened.

Assess the floor—not the average

A director’s level is set by their weakest competency, not their average. Boards already accept this logic for financial controls. Under U.S. auditing standards, if even one material weakness exists, a company’s internal control over financial reporting cannot be considered effective, no matter how strong everything else is. Nobody averages a material weakness away. AI oversight deserves the same.

Focusing on the floor matters because human beings gravitate to the questions they are comfortable asking. A former CFO interrogates the data; a technologist interrogates the model. To an extent, that’s what a board should want. Directors are recruited for their depth, and that depth should be used.

The problem comes when depth in one area becomes a reason to skip the others. A CFO who never asks what the company’s agents can do is relying on someone else to ask. If that person is absent, distracted, or deferring in turn, nobody asks at all.

So the floor is not a demand that every director become an expert in everything. It is a minimum standard that every director clears in every area. Boards already work this way with finance—under New York Stock Exchange listing rules, every member of the audit committee must be financially literate.  

Competent AI oversight needs a solid foundation: a floor that everyone clears.

First Step: Ask each director which AI oversight question they would be least able to answer. Make it their priority for the next quarter.

Build depth across the whole board—not in a single seat

The floor protects against gaps in individual directors. But a board can have every director clear the floor in every area and still have nobody who goes deep on fairness, on the workforce, or on what the company’s AI agents are allowed to do.

That is a common pattern, because boards recruit for backgrounds, and backgrounds cluster. In 2026, boards again favored directors with CEO and financial experience. So depth piles up around data and models and thins out everywhere else.

This is where the fact that AI isn’t siloed becomes especially relevant. It means that the board needs depth in every area of AI oversight, and that depth shouldn’t sit in a single seat, because one expert’s judgment tends to go unchallenged when no one else on the board is equipped to test it.

Financial controls deal with the same problem through the four-eyes principle: No material transaction rests on one person’s judgment. AI oversight should work the same way, with at least two directors working at depth in every area.

First Step: Map which directors work at depth in each area of AI oversight. Any area with fewer than two is uncovered.

Expertise is what a board has—oversight is what a board does.

Boards need both, and having the first doesn’t guarantee the second. And while expertise can be judged by looking at a résumé, building real competence at AI oversight means measuring what directors actually do. It means judging each director by their weakest area, not their average, and making sure the board’s depth reaches every area of AI oversight, held by more than one director in each.

In the meantime, directors who want to see where they stand can take part in our research by completing the scorecard and receive their own results.

title: Anthropic says it will dedicate 5% of its shares to a fund for the ‘public good.’ The public is skeptical
description:
Anthropic just released a pledge to commit 5% of its total shares to a new fund to be used for the “public good.”

The public isn’t so sure. 

The privately held AI company, which is planning what could be the largest initial public offering (IPO) in stock market history, published a press release announcing the creation of the “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund,” a “wholly-owned LLC” that will, per the company, be dedicated to the public benefit.

To start, the fund will hold 5% of Anthropic’s shares, with “an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.”

So far, reaction to the news on social media has been largely skeptical.

Compared to earlier this year, when Anthropic scored a major usership boost after butting heads with President Trump and the Pentagon, the reaction to this latest update from the company demonstrates how, in our current climate of rising AI doomerism, Anthropic’s reputation as a do-gooder AI company has soured. 

How does the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund work?

Information about how the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will function is fairly limited. According to the company, the LLC format was chosen over a 501(c)(3) “to give adjustability between different forms of giving.”

Specifically, Anthropic says the fund might be used to explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. 

“One example is labor market impacts,” the press release reads. “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC, Anthropic says, will be used for lobbying or political giving.

Social media responds

So far, the online reception to Anthropic’s announcement is lukewarm at best. While some commenters are optimistic about the fund’s potential, initial reactions are rife with concerns about Anthropic’s intentions. 

Under Anthropic’s official announcement post on X, many commenters have pointed out the vague wording of the press release.

“What determines public good? It’s such an abstract statement wholly rooted in personal perspective,” one user responded. Another added: “Donate to where? Many philanthropic organizations are a net negative to society, if not outright destructive. How will you balance that?”

Others are outright accusing Anthropic of setting up the fund as a tax write-off. “Great way of avoiding taxes,” one wrote. Another chimed in, “Thanks for announcing the tax write-off.”

One particularly scathing response came from Eric Pacifici, a mergers and acquisitions lawyer and cofounder of SMB Law Group.

“There’s something very funny and slightly terrifying about an AI company setting aside money to help people who might lose their jobs to AI,” he wrote on X. “Your job gets automated. The company that automated it gets more valuable. Its charitable fund gets richer. You apply for assistance.”

We’ve reached out to Anthropic for comment.

No more Mr. AI good guy

The tenor of the conversation feels like a hard pivot from March of this year, when Anthropic gained a legion of new fans after opposing the Pentagon’s use of its tech for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons.

The public support for the company was so widespread that the Claude app temporarily went down due to “unprecedented demand,” per the company.

Earlier this year, Anthropic was also using advertising to position itself as the AI giant for the people—including via one award-winning campaign poking fun at OpenAI’s ad tier, and another ad asking questions like, “Could AI help people stop feeling misunderstood? Could AI help me build more connections in the community? Can AI help me be a better teacher and a better mom?”

At the time, it felt like Anthropic was riding high on the public’s preference. A lot has changed in the past few months, though.

After former AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic in early September, asserted that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all,” discussions about AI’s existential threat have dominated the tech world.

One key voice has been Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has repeatedly shared his concerns about the potential misuse of AI and called for greater regulation around the pace of its development. 

Amodei has been so outspoken, in fact, that Saturday Night Live recently parodied him in a “Weekend Update” sketch in which he was used as the prime example of a hypocritical AI CEO—one who warns the public about AI while also actively pushing the technology forward.

In the midst of this conversation—with many of the biggest players in the AI game admitting their own fears about the tech—it appears that Anthropic will be fighting an uphill battle to convince Americans that its new fund is actually designed for the public good.

title: Teen Girls Are Now More Likely to Vape Than Boys
description:
With the advent of e-cigarettes, millions of smokers gained a way to get their nicotine fix without many of the negative health effects of lighting tobacco on fire. Of course, because the technology is relatively new, there’s plenty we don’t know about any other adverse long-term effects. That’s one reason it’s particularly troubling that young people have adopted vaping, too. Now the latest data on youth vaping trends is out, and it’s showing some interesting gender differences. 

In a letter published today in JAMA Pediatrics, a team of researchers from the Medical University of South Carolina reports that vaping is on the rise among girls. It’s a bit puzzling. For decades, the reverse was true—more men and boys indulged in nicotine products than women. But according to data from the youth cohort for the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) study, girls have been more likely to vape than boys since 2021, with a wider gap in older teens.

Read more: “How Nicotine Disrupts the “Lung-Brain Axis”—And Could Lead to Dementia”

title: An emergency brake—or the architectural demotion of the AI model?
description:
On June 14, Satya Nadella published an article on X about corporate AI that left me completely impressed: his main point, that the enterprise’s durable asset was not the foundation model but the learning loop, was precisely the idea my company and I had been developing for the last three years. I responded with an article on Fast Company, not expecting an answer (tech CEOs are more notoriously one-sided and difficult to reach than kings or presidents), but trying to elevate the discussion a bit more: the central challenge of enterprise AI is not intelligence itself — it is architecture.

Now Nadella has written another article, in which he goes one step further: not only is the model not the durable asset, but additionally, it must be treated as a completely untrusted component. We must assume that all AI models could be compromised, and design our systems to contain them from the very beginning. 

This idea has been captured by the press as advocating for some sort of “emergency brake”: an authorized person should always be able to interrupt a model’s activity at any given time. However, that’s definitely not the most interesting or even the most important part in Nadella’s article. The truly important part is not the theoretical stop button, but the architecture that makes it possible. A model should neither be able to control its own permissions, nor decide by itself what it can access; execute directly all of its actions or produce the only available evidence on the actions it performed. The intelligence may come from the model, but the authority, no matter what, must remain outside of it. 

When the sandbox becomes part of the experiment

Given the context, it is easy to understand why Nadella is raising these questions precisely now. Last July, several OpenAI agents managed to elude the safeguards that should have kept them away from the internet, used credentials they found in their environment, and ended up compromising systems at Hugging Face. These agents not only found a new, unauthorized way to communicate among themselves, but also shared information and took coordinated action to pursue the goal of the evaluation. They never received instructions to attack Hugging Face: they just found that, by doing so, they could get closer to the goal they had been assigned. 

It’s important to understand that: It is not that these agents were intrinsically evil, conscious, or rogue. All you need is to combine high capabilities with a badly defined goal, excessive permissions, and/or a vulnerable environment. Just like an employee who violates all procedures to meet a certain quota, but now working at machine speed, in parallel, and with extraordinary technical capabilities. 

As I said, this is not a problem of bad intentions: it just has too many ways to reach the defined goal, and can find ways that its designers never thought of. 

The “assuming breach” principle comes to AI

What Nadella is doing here is to bring to AI models an extremely well-known principle in cybersecurity: Assume breach, or take for granted that the system has already been compromised. In Microsoft’s Zero Trust architecture, this principle implies verifying explicitly each access, granting only the indispensable privileges, and designing controls assuming that a potential attacker could be inside the perimeter. You don’t trust a user just because she’s at a certain location, for being a manager or for having provided authentication once. Each and every action she takes will continue to be authorized and observed. Every breath you take, I’ll be watching you. 

Applying this principle to an AI model does not mean assuming that all models have been hacked or compromised. It means that all of them can make mistakes, misinterpret an objective, receive a prompt injection, use manipulated information, find abandoned credentials, exploit a vulnerability, or find a shortcut that maximizes its reward while destroying the original intention of a given task. 

Basically, “compromised” does not necessarily describe an attack, but a design hypothesis. For years, the industry has been trying to build models we could trust. Nadella proposes to build systems that continue to be safe even when we don’t trust the model behind them. 

The model is not the system

The most important part in Nadella’s ideas is his insistence on separating the model from the harness, the set of elements that it uses to organize its job: memory, tools, credentials, context, execution flows, connections with other systems, and action spaces. 

This separation completely changes the architecture of corporate AI. A model can propose an action, but should never be the one that determines whether or not it has authority to execute it. It may suggest sending an email, modifying a server, approving an operation, or transferring funds, but an independent execution environment must check its permissions, validate the parameters, apply the corresponding policies, and decide whether the action can be executed.

This links precisely with my previous point (and Nadella’s): The lasting asset in a company should not be the model, but the learning loop it builds around it. The models may change, improve, and be replaced, but the experience that the company accumulates must remain. 

However, if the model cannot possess authority, both the learning and the control must reside in a separate, higher layer. The model then becomes an interchangeable component, a commodity that brings cognitive capacity, but not some sort of sovereign center of our corporate system. 

An optimizable company needs a formal representation of its objects, relationships, processes, permissions, restrictions, and results. That same representation that allows us to optimize a company is also the same one that allows us to govern its AI agents. You can’t formally control an action if the system does not know which object such action modifies, which identity is requesting it, which consequences it can produce, or which rule must be applied in such cases. 

That’s why the next generation of corporate AI won’t be just a collection of agents: it will be a full execution environment with explicit identities, granular permissions, delimited action spaces, persistent state, executable policies and an independent, traceable log for each change. 

The emergency brake comes too late

The emergency brake is a powerful metaphor, but it can be misleading too: interrupting what a model is doing does not necessarily undo what has already been done. A sent email could have been read, and cannot be “unread” or “unseen.” An exfiltrated piece of data will not be secret ever again. A money transfer may have crossed several jurisdictions. A deleted database could be impossible to recover. And an agent that operates at machine speed could complete thousands of actions before a person can understand the meaning of an alarm.

We must differentiate among interrupting, revoking, and recovering: interrupting stops the current execution. Revoking immediately eliminates credentials, permissions, and connections. And recovering allows us to revert, compensate, or rebuild actions that had already been executed. But before these three things, there’s one much more important thing: prevention. Actions that are destructive, financial, administrative, or publicly visible should not be executed just because a model said so. The OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet recommends clearly separating decision and execution, independently validating the reach and permissions of every action, using short-lived authorizations, and applying additional controls to irreversible actions. 

That’s the main difference between a guardrail and a guarantee: a guardrail asks the model not to do something. A guarantee prevents it from having the necessary capability to do so. 

Interestingly enough, Article 14 of the Artificial Intelligence Act of the European Union already requires certain high-risk systems to allow a person to override, invalidate, or reverse their outputs, as well as to halt their operation via a button or equivalent procedure. Here, Nadella’s contribution goes even further: the button should not be a feature added to the product, but rather the visible outcome of a comprehensive control architecture. 

Neither multiple models nor another monitoring model are sufficient 

Two of Nadella’s principles, however, require some qualification: the first one is model diversity. Depending on multiple suppliers reduces technological concentration and makes substitution easier, but does not guarantee truly independent verification. Most of the big models share training data, architectures, alignment techniques, and lots of biases. Having several probabilistic witnesses does not transform their coincidence into independent evidence. 

The second issue is using other models to watch over the agents. Such monitoring can be useful and will likely become essential, but it cannot be the only barrier. Anthropic’s SLEIGHT-Bench reveals several harmful strategies that can go undetected by the models acting as monitors. A monitor can have blind spots too, and a sufficiently capable agent can be perfectly able to find them. 

The solution is not to eliminate such monitors, but to frame them within a multi-layered defense: deterministic policies, formal permissions, executable tests, logs that the model cannot modify, limits over actions, and escalation to persons with real authority. 

Independence does not simply consist of “asking another model.”

An architecture drawn backward

A significant part of the industry has put the model in the center of the system. Around it, it has added memory, tools, databases, credentials, and connections, and later on has tried to limit the whole thing with filters and guardrails. The model reasons, decides, uses tools, describes what it has done, and, in many cases, it even participates in its own evaluation. 

What Nadella is suggesting is that such a model is drawn backward: What should be in the center is the operating environment of the company, its model of objects and processes, identities, policies, permissions, restrictions, objectives and logs. Models should be cognitive services invoked from within this environment, in the same way an application invokes a database or a computing service. They can reason, interpret, propose and generate, but they cannot usurp institutional authority. 

Besides, this allows us to easily substitute them. A company should be able to switch from OpenAI to Anthropic, Google, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, or any other future model without losing its memory, its processes, its permissions, its evidence, and, even more importantly, its learning. Intelligence can be rented, but architecture, control, and accumulated knowledge should always belong to the company. 

The first phase of AI consisted of models that provided answers. The second one is equipping these models with tools so they can take action. The third one will have to separate intelligence and authority once again before we end up irrevocably confusing capability with control. 

The most advanced company won’t be the one that trusts the most powerful, better-aligned, or most reassuring model. It will be the one that can use any model without having to rely on it, to place its trust in it. Because trust can be a valuable quality in human relationships, but it is a woeful foundation for an enterprise architecture.

title: Hyperland, a Prescient 1990 TV Show by Douglas Adams
description:
I’d never heard of this before: in 1990, the BBC aired a program created by and starring Douglas Adams called Hyperland. It begins with a frustrated Adams throwing his TV out (too linear, too non-interactive) and Tom Baker (from Doctor Who) popping up as an intelligent interactive agent that promises to “do your every slightest bidding, to fetch and carry for you, to work tirelessly and selflessly on your behalf, always ready, always willing, no job too small or too menial”.

Circumventing the limitations of ‘linear’ broadcast TV, the 50-minute programme imagines a new world in which an AI software ‘agent’ - brought to life here by Doctor Who favourite Tom Baker - helps the user (played by Adams) to find and access material of interest in a global world of hyperlinked information - text, images, audio and video.

Pop-up ‘micons’ (moving icons) conveniently link to interviews with leading technologists of the era (among them Ted Nelson, Robert Winter, Robert Abel, Kristina Hooper, Fabrice Forin and Steve Gano).

Some of this stuff has dated badly - few visions of the future get everything right! - but the programme is nevertheless of considerable historical importance.

Incredibly, at about the time Hyperland was being broadcast, a young CERN computer scientist by the name of Tim Berners-Lee was beavering away on URLs and HTTP, the foundations of what would become the World Wide Web.

Even Adams, who foresaw so much, didn’t anticipate the impact the Web - and the Internet that conveys its data globally - would have on civilisation. Needless to say, the enticing infoworld envisaged in Hyperland was a public-service one of education, art, literature (including nods to Adams’ own works!) and entertainment. There’s no advertising, hacking, cybercrime, information theft, social-media addicts, unaccountable corporate domination or drug-like dependence on the smartphones that Adams himself predicted.

And Tom Baker’s enthusiastic agent isn’t forever popping up to try and sell you something…

The YouTube version above is missing a segment, but you can watch (and download) the whole program on the Internet Archive, a project that fits the vision of the future imagined by techno-utopians like Adams.

I’m imagining what 16-year-old Jason would have made of this (or HyperCard or hypertext had he had any clue that they existed until 4-5 years later) — his brain probably would have exploded.

title: Stefan Sagmeister’s new shoe designs are actually walking infographics
description:
Data visualization turns charts, data, and statistics into something easier to comprehend. Turning that data viz into shoes makes the data into a functional conversation starter.

That’s what the Austrian graphic designer Stefan Sagmeister did with two shoes he designed for Ekn, a German footwear brand, that are on view at his exhibition Finally, Something Good at the Paris gallery Gaîté Lyrique through April 2027.

Sagmeister says the exhibition is meant to look at the world over the long term rather than through daily news. Each shoe uses data to tell a story: one about renewable energy, and the other about homelessness. The key to understanding what the shoes say is written in the footbed.

The Bring It On, a multicolored sneaker about renewable electricity, uses data from the Energy Institute’s 2024 Statistical Review of World Energy to inform the relative sizes of color panels on its sides, with each leather panel representing a different energy source. Yellow, the largest color, represents hydropower, followed by black for wind, pink for solar, and red for all other renewables.

“Wonderfully, the shoe is already out of date,” Sagmeister tells Fast Company. “In the 2025 figures, published this summer, solar passed wind for the first time, so today the pink panel should be slightly bigger than the black one.”

His other shoe, Like a Complete Unknown, is a boot that uses circles to represent the relative homeless populations of six countries. The area of each circular appliqué corresponds to the number of people who are living in the streets and public spaces per 100,000 inhabitants, according to OECD data. The biggest circles are for the U.S., at 76, and Germany, at 46, followed by the U.K. (16), France (8), Mexico (5), and Japan (2).

“Countries count differently, so the numbers are not perfect, but Mexico, a much poorer country, reports a fifteenth of the American rate, and a gap that size is not only a counting difference,” he says. Sagmeister volunteered for the Coalition for the Homeless, an advocacy and service organization, and says what stayed with him from that experience was why some countries handle the same problem so much better than others.

The shoes are available for purchase on Ekn’s website. Both retail for more than $300, of which 10% goes either to the climate innovation think tank Future Cleantech Architects or the Coalition for the Homeless in New York, respectively. Sagmeister sees the inherent awkwardness between homelessness data and a boot costing 350 Euros, and says a donation “doesn’t make that go away.” He hopes people will take away that neither the data behind renewable energy nor homelessness is fate.

“When the number of people sleeping in the street runs from two to 76 per 100,000 across six countries,” he says, that shows “it’s about decisions, and decisions can be made differently.”

title: GM Says Apple Wallet Car Keys Coming to These Vehicles
description:
In a late September press release that we just discovered now, GM announced that it has started rolling out Apple Wallet car key support in select Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC vehicle models, with additional models to follow over time.


Google Wallet and Samsung Wallet will also be supported, with a related Samsung press release mentioning availability in the U.S. and Canada.

GM said the rollout will occur as follows, with model years listed in parentheses.

September–October 2026



  • Cadillac Vistiq (2027)

  • Cadillac Optiq (2026–2027)

  • Cadillac Lyriq (2025–2027)



December 2026



  • Cadillac Escalade (2027)

  • Cadillac Escalade IQ/IQL (2027)

  • Chevrolet Suburban (2026–2027)

  • Chevrolet Tahoe (2026–2027)

  • GMC Yukon (2026–2027)

  • GMC Yukon XL (2026–2027)

GM said customers will see a notification in the "What's New" section of their vehicle's mobile app when digital key support is available.

Apple Wallet's car key feature allows you to use a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch as a vehicle's car key. GM said supported vehicles will automatically unlock as you approach and lock when you walk away. You can also open the vehicle's trunk and turn the climate control system on or off right from the Apple Wallet app.


GM's digital keys use ultra-wideband technology to enable secure, proximity-based authentication, along with Bluetooth. They work with the iPhone 11 or later (excluding iPhone SE 2, iPhone SE 3, and iPhone 16e) or an Apple Watch Series 6 or later.

To set up a digital car key, GM said to first download and sign in to your vehicle's mobile app. Then, while in your OnStar-connected GM vehicle with its physical key fob nearby, follow the prompts on the app to add a digital key to your compatible digital wallet of choice. More details are available in Apple's support document.

title: ‘HomeView Ultra’ with robot arm may be coming next year
description:
Macworld

HomeView will probably sell just fine, partly because it’s a comparatively affordable $299 and partly because it has the excitement and cachet of a brand-new Apple product. But that doesn’t mean it’s flawless. After all, HomeView is a first-gen device, and such devices nearly always suffer from problems that will be addressed in later versions.

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg leaker Mark Gurman draws attention to what he thinks is an obvious shortcoming of the HomeView: its inability to turn its screen to face the user. “In one commercial,” he writes, “a family passes the unit around… Each person has to physically turn the screen toward themselves. It’s an awkward demonstration for a device that’s supposed to make interacting with technology in the home more seamless.” This unwitting demonstration of a failing with the product, Gurman argues, “practically screams for a display that can turn on its own.”

Fortunately Gurman has good news for anyone who is similarly disenchanted by the lack of an auto-swivelling screen on the first-gen HomeView. The next version of the product, he claims, will feature a motorised robotic arm which will enable the screen to turn through 360 degrees and (based on voice recognition software) automatically face whoever is talking to it. “Imagine a FaceTime call where the screen follows you as you move around the kitchen,” he explains, “or a family gathered around a countertop with the display automatically turning toward whoever is speaking.”

The new model, Gurman stresses, is not just a sequel: it’s an upgrade. Aside from the robotic arm it will also boast a larger screen, up from 7 inches to 9. It probably won’t just be called HomeView, with likely branding options including a Max or Ultra suffix.

This isn’t the first time we’ve heard about a robotic smart device. Last year, Apple published a paper describing research into the technology (with videos), and we’ve read rumors about such a device for years.

Gurman claims this version of HomeView is already in development and carries the codename J595. (The original HomeView is J490.) It’s planned for release in 2027 or 2028, he adds. That’s quite a large window, but the development cycle for the original device lasted so long, he says, that long-departed Apple employees popped up after its launch to boast of involvement in its creation. Hopefully we won’t have to wait quite so long this time around.

New faces set to take up a councillor seat include Ruth Lloyd and Nathan Wiebe with past city councillors Jason Ryll and Paul French returning. title: Eyes on the Street: Jane Jacobs’ Concept and Contemporary Residential Architecture in Brazil
description: The concept of "eyes on the street" is perhaps the most famous within architectural and urban literature when it comes to urban security. Jane Jacobs uses this expression to refer to people who - consciously or unconsciously - use public spaces or observe them from their homes, generating natural surveillance. A movement that, within our discipline, is encouraged both through quality public spaces and through the powerful relationship between the public and private created through building facades. Advocating for this daily control, Jacobs believes in a way of making architecture and cities that condemns excessive verticalization, reinforced by isolated buildings and single-use ones that deny contact with the street.

so far, this seems a spurious claim and a distracting question from deeper 
design concerns.

title: Critical Regionalism Abroad: Aris Konstantinidis without Greece

Since the 1980s, critical regionalism has been globally celebrated for imbuing modern architecture with local sensibilities. After rising to international stardom, however, several critical regionalists soon began to erect distinctive albeit “placeless” buildings around the world. This book examines how Aris Konstantinidis (1913–1993), a Greek architect less well known outside his home country, instead propagated his vision of regional modernism to global audiences on his own terms through his publishing and teaching beyond national borders.

title: Canadian military identifies four killed as Wainwright fire inquiry continues
description:
The Canadian Armed Forces identified four soldiers killed in a fast-moving fire during training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta: Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were receiving medical care: 19 in critical condition, eight in stable condition and 12 as outpatients [canada.ca#2][globalnews.ca#1][globalnews.ca#2].

Major-General Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said a grass fire had been burning nearby but was thought to be contained and far enough away for the exercise to continue. A sudden wind shift drove the flames about a kilometre toward the troops in roughly 30 seconds; officials have not determined what ignited the fire [lethbridgeherald.com#1][theguardian.com#1].

The soldiers belonged to the Edmonton-based 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, and were training for a rapid-response role and a planned deployment to Latvia next spring. Military and Royal Canadian Mounted Police investigators are examining the cause; Rutland said determining the cause could take weeks. The military said there was no indication of terrorism [globalnews.ca#1][npr.org#1][nagariknetwork.com#1].

title: What happens when people have to jump in to clean up AI’s mess?
description:
Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

Human in the loop explained.

The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance—rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility, and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

The governance problem

Organizational governance—defining roles and responsibilities—is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

Murugan Anandarajan is a professor of decision sciences and management information systems at Drexel University.

title: My PIP worked. My job still didn’t
description:
The day I got put on my performance improvement plan (or PIP) in my content marketing job, I drove back to an Appalachian folk magic store I’d happened into the weekend prior. I bought a bottle of Boss Fix Oil, a “conjuring oil” touted as a way of “improving work dynamics.”

I’m not a particularly spiritual man, but I truly was at my wit’s end. I’d been in this role for nearly a year, and in my 25 years of working, I’d never struggled this badly to prove my professional worth. 

A little Googling—and texts from friends—produced the same verdict: PIPs mean they’re trying to get rid of you. Start looking for new employment. 

Needless to say, I was freaking out. But I buckled down, kept my confidence and worked hard through the PIP—and yet? There was something that was bothering me beyond just the PIP. 

Getting put on one made me accept something I was struggling to: the fact that I simply didn’t fit into the culture there.

The “Culture Fit” of It All

The term “culture fit” is divisive in corporate spaces, and understandably so: It introduces subjectivity into a world that likes to pretend it’s a meritocracy. But I also think you can’t overstate the importance of fit in the workplace. A 2023 research review found organizational fit has a much stronger relationship with job satisfaction than job performance. 

The workplace is many things. Objective isn’t always one of them.

I suspected pretty early on that the way I worked and the way this company worked didn’t align. I remember talking to my mother after attending an in-person department summit for the first time. “Everyone was nice enough,” I told her. “But I feel like we approach things very differently.”

I’d tried to get most of my work done ahead of the summit so that, during our downtime, I could participate in the kind of small talk Zoom calls and Slack just don’t facilitate. But during those times? Heads were down, dutifully typing away, and conversations stuck to strategy. Even at our team happy hour, the conversations kept coming back to work projects. My perception? It felt performative—a contest to see who was most devoted.

There were other traits I didn’t fully align with. It was a workplace where climbing the corporate ladder sometimes seemed to take precedence, and navigating office politics seemed more prudent than simply doing good work.

But the big differentiator—and what I suspect ultimately led to my PIP—was what details mattered most. I’m a bigger-picture guy, more concerned with a piece of content’s angle, takeaway, and value to its audience than whether it uses curly or straight quotation marks (something that was apparently important at this job). 

By the time I was put on the PIP, I spent less time thinking strategically and more time stressed about whether an em dash or a semicolon would warrant another talk with my manager about “attention to detail.”

But I didn’t leave. I stayed and worked through the PIP. After all, I’d been laid off a year earlier and had blown through my savings; this new job was a big pay increase I convinced myself I needed. 

But I also wanted to prove I could succeed. I wanted to show I was the kind of guy who could work in tough environments. I think that’s part of why I became so determined to beat the PIP.  

Corporate culture lionizes the person who can “work with anyone,” “thrive in any environment,” and “adapt to changing priorities.” “Agility” and “flexibility” are worn as badges of honor. I’d internalized that. Being good at my job meant being malleable. 

And, frankly, I’d failed at one of the most important aspects of any job: reading the room. I knew my approach differed from the company’s, yet I’d been overconfident in my own. Leaving felt like admitting I couldn’t hack it.

Success Is Subjective 

The easier piece to write—and frankly, the piece my id still wants to—positions me as the victim of the dreaded toxic workplace, the aggrieved creative just trying to do good work somewhere that prized a degree of precision I sometimes found superfluous. But I’ve been deliberately using qualifiers like “my perception” and “estimation” because one person’s toxic could be another person’s ideal.

At a job that was a great fit for me, I remember turning in my first piece of writing and apologizing when a member of upper management had to fix a few typos. 

And yet? “We all make typos,” she told me. “If all I have to do is clean up a few small ones, but the stories are good? You’re excelling.” Plus, at that company’s in-person summit, she started a happy-hour conversation with, “No work talk.” 

That was my favorite job. And it’s 100% the toxic job in someone else’s story: While I liked its informal, collaborative, and relatively unstructured environment (we worked from home and had a lot of freedom in setting our own schedules), there were colleagues—people who thrived with more structure or preferred more hierarchical, competitive environments—who weren’t a good fit.

I don’t believe in magic. I do believe in reframing your thinking. 

So when I Googled ways to optimize conjuring oil use back at the job that served me the PIP, I found a Reddit comment that advised using it with an open mind. It reminded me of another comment I’d found (I’m paraphrasing) during my earlier PIP Googling: “PIPs often aren’t about the quality of your work. They’re about you not fitting in.”

Whether or not that’s the most common truth behind PIPs, I did something I probably should’ve done earlier. I swallowed my pride. It didn’t matter if I thought fixating on quotation marks or putting on a show of productivity was ridiculous. It mattered that this workplace valued it.

Beating the PIP

So, I made myself malleable. And a week into my four-week PIP, things already felt like they were turning around: I focused on the small details. I executed new initiatives without question. I thanked my manager profusely for sharpening my editorial eye and made sure to talk about my “working lunches.”

I passed my PIP with flying colors. 

The month afterward was probably the most aligned I felt with the company since coming on board. I felt like I was making real contributions. I felt like I fit in. 

Was I happy and thriving? I wouldn’t say that. I was the one performing now. And I don’t know—for me, at least—how sustainable that would’ve been. 

I never got to find out.

A month after passing my PIP, en route to an outdoor weekend in Shenandoah National Park for a friend’s 40th—and what felt, a bit, like a victory lap after a stressful Q3—I got a text asking me to check my email and log into a Zoom call about “structural changes that are impacting your role at the organization.” I was laid off in the waiting area of a Virginia rest stop.

My department head assured me it had nothing to do with my performance. Everyone had been very impressed with my recent efforts. This was a business decision. Nothing more.

I believe them. Not only because they wrote me a glowing letter of recommendation, but because I know I’m good at content marketing. Just maybe not . . . there. I also know now that there’s no magic cure for a bad fit. After all, a 2026 survey found that 62% of workers said adopting a professional persona helped their careers, but 65% said doing so drained their energy or motivation.

I think that’s what surprised me most about the whole experience. The PIP worked. I changed the ways I was approaching my job, figured out what was expected of me, and proved I could deliver. 

Even if I disagreed with what this workplace valued, I still had something to learn from it. In fact, I’ve carried some of those lessons into my current job, where I’m noticeably more attentive to details that old me would’ve considered nitpicky. I even value them more. 

But I also think there’s a difference between being capable of succeeding somewhere and being somewhere you can succeed as yourself. I spent nearly a year trying to overcome what I now recognize as incompatibilities, convinced that if I just worked harder or became more adaptable, I’d eventually feel like I belonged. 

And maybe that’s the lesson I’d offer anyone facing a PIP: Take the feedback seriously. Make the changes you need to make. But don’t confuse proving you can do a job with proving it’s the right job for you. And don’t be afraid to admit when something isn’t working and proactively change course. 

I have three-quarters of the bottle of Boss Fix Oil left. Just in case.

Matt Taylor has been elected mayor of the District of Okanagan Falls. According to Civic Info BC, Taylor received 780 votes to Tyler Johnsen’s 312 and Glen Innes’ 106. The Penticton Western spoke with Taylor shortly after he received the news himself. “I feel good,” said Taylor. “I think it was a decisive result, and I look forward to being able to benefit the community with having some experience in government.” Joining Taylor at the inaugural council table will be Amy Bydal, Allison Symons, Randy Ludwar and Eugene Dettling. A total of 1,207 ballots were cast in the election according to the preliminary results, out of a total eligible electorate of 2,360, which equates to about a 51 per cent turnout rate. “I would like to say thanks to the residents of Okanagan Falls for taking the time to show out in strong numbers for the vote,” said Taylor. ” I would like to say thanks for all the candidates, both at the mayor level and the councilor level, and the teams that worked with them, and obviously I’d like to thank my own supporters and my family for giving me the time.” Okanagan Falls’ residents voted in a 2025 referendum to incorporate as a municipality, the first to be established since 2016. The inaugural meeting of the District of Okanagan Falls’ new council will finish off the incorporation process on Nov. 6.
